strengths: Allie models human chess playing more holistically by also predicting think time and special decisions such as resignation, and these prediction outputs can be used to parameterize an MCTS search; this time-adaptive search proves to be crucial for closing the skill gap between Allie and the human opponent, as shown in the human study.

Allie achieves good move-matching accuracy across a wider range of Elo ratings and closer skill calibration to human players than prior work; the fact that Allie can play at a grandmaster level (2500 Elo) is an impressive achievement given that behavior cloning on human data typically yields sub-expert policies.

The authors include GPT 3.5 as a challenging baseline; GPT 3.5's move‑matching accuracy is remarkable, and Allie's performance is still slightly better while requiring much fewer parameters and enabling search.

Allie's architecture is sensibly designed: the use of move tokens and history is a natural way of representing a board position for a transformer model, avoiding the need for a visual representation; the use of "soft tokens" to encode each player's Elo ratings allows conditioning on skill level, and taking the final decoder layer output and parameterizing each prediction using separate linear layers is a clean design.
The user study was a nice addition, demonstrating Allie's skill calibration in real human games and collecting survey results on how enjoyable and human‑like Allie (and the other baselines) felt.
The paper presents an original approach to human‑like play modeling and answers most of the reviewer’s questions.

The idea of using a transformer to solve chess predates the current LLM craze; while most ideas are not novel, the combination and execution are the most successful so far, and adding the ponder time is done very well.
The experiments look to be done well and the paper flows well; adding the human studies was a good move to really show an improvement over Maia.
Chess AI has had a resurgence in the last few years; this work could aid that work and shows a path for many other turn‑based games, indicating potential significance.
Shows strong and accurate performance across a wide range of Elo scores.
Strong performance compared to Maia, which is also human aligned.
Thorough analysis on different aspects of the algorithm (accuracy of move prediction, accuracy of pondering times, accuracy of value estimate).
Extensive human study.
Proposes novel ideas for developing human‑like agents by considering not only move accuracy but also non‑move behaviors of human players, such as pondering time and when to resign.
Helps bridge the gap in developing human‑aligned AIs, as strong AI agents may exhibit non‑interpretable behaviors.
Compares favorably with state‑of‑the‑art agents, MAIA and GPT‑3.5, achieving better results.
The objectives of the paper are clearly defined, and the paper sticks close to these objectives.
The writing and presentation of the paper are clear and of good quality; no visible typos in the main text.
Modeling the pondering time and resignation and utilizing the time prediction for adaptive MCTS are novel ideas; the invention of soft tokens for strength conditioning is a fresh idea.

The presented evaluation methods and metrics seem rigorous; the work complements the offline human alignment evaluation with surveys consisting of quantitative and qualitative feedback from online users.
weaknesses: The discussion of Maia in the introduction and related work seems lacking/misleading; it is not fair to say existing systems are not "human‑aligned" and relevant prior work (NeurIPS ’21, KDD ’22) should be cited.

Published Maia models do not include think time, resignation, or history; archived submissions extend Maia in these ways, and a recent NeurIPS ’24 paper "Maia‑2: A Unified Model for Human‑AI Alignment in Chess" should be discussed; additionally, Allie's 355M parameters are more than an order of magnitude bigger than Maia, a size difference not mentioned.
The paper should better frame its contribution as predicting human‑like outputs that enable augmenting a behavior‑cloned model with search, rather than focusing on superficial differences.

Adding MCTS search introduces a non‑human‑like element; there is not enough evidence that humans search the game tree in an MCTS‑like manner, so claims about only relying on human data should be toned down; it would be helpful to report move‑matching accuracy as a function of search time, explain how the constant 'c' in the rollouts function was chosen, and show sensitivity of results to that choice.
It is unclear why Allie's value estimates are expected to match Stockfish; it would be more sensible to compare Allie's value estimate to the actual game outcome rather than Stockfish's assessment.
The reviewer asks how adaptive search does better than non‑adaptive (AlphaZero‑like) search against 2500 Elo players and whether the non‑adaptive search time is bounded.
The reviewer questions whether the soft‑token representation for Elo is sparse, asking if it suffers from a lack of examples associated with each value or is represented differently internally.

The loss function does not mention normalization or weights to balance the different loss terms; this could be an issue given the very different nature of the terms (e.g., log‑likelihood of next move vs. MSA of think‑time prediction).
The term "human‑aligned" is not good in this paper; it may be interpreted in the AI‑alignment sense, so a different term should be used.

It is unclear how the <resign> token can be used in practice; a false positive rate of 0.1% could lead to ~2% over 20 moves, and a single bad resign could end a game; the reviewer asks whether resign prediction was used in the user studies and how it looks in real gameplay.
The lack of code is concerning; the reviewer’s rating is contingent on the authors fulfilling their promises about code release.

The work is entirely based on offline data recorded from human gameplays, limiting the scope for human‑aligned AI; large parts of the data were removed for training (downsampling low‑Elo games, removing transitions under time pressure), suggesting that training ALLIE‑like agents requires a specific training regimen.
There does not seem to be any related work on skill calibration cited.

The claim that ALLIE has a "reliable board value estimate" is misleading; Fig 3 shows a Pearson r = 0.697 which is already quite noisy, and many positions have low correlation (r < 0.3); the reviewer requests mean absolute error values.

GPT‑3.5 has comparable move‑matching accuracy on higher‑Elo games; the reviewer suggests a more in‑depth comparison and wonders whether a fine‑tuned GPT‑3.5 on the same dataset would result in a human‑aligned agent.

Novelty is very limited; the paper directly applies the transformer architecture to chess and only introduces new outputs (pondering time, resignation); it does not explicitly explain why the transformer is better than MAIA's residual networks, and the larger parameter size may increase inference time, so fairness of experiments should be reconsidered, including comparison of inference time and parameter counts under the same hardware.

The evaluation set excludes moves made under time pressure (remaining time < 30 s); these blitz moves might reflect human intuition and should be included; also, incorporating remaining time as an input to the model could avoid needing to exclude such moves.
The method is only applied to chess; it is unclear whether it can be generalized to other games, and the authors should include other games to demonstrate effectiveness.
Minor typo in abstract: "... resignations In offline evaluations," should be "... resignations in offline evaluations,".
The time spent for each move should be recorded in the game history, but this is not explicitly stated in the main text; the reviewer asks the authors to address it.

The design of ALLIE is akin to AlphaGo [1] without the self‑play phase; training the neural networks entirely on human data and applying MCTS for policy improvement is not seen as an algorithmic advancement.

The authors stress the necessity of adaptive search for skill calibration, but failure to match grandmaster level may simply reflect a lack of strength; it is unclear if adaptive search is truly necessary or if improved performance is due to increased search depth.
Because users knew they were playing against an AI before filling out the survey, the human alignment result from the user study might not be as objective as a Turing test would be.

It would better support the superiority of adaptive search in skill calibration if ALLIE with adaptive search were compared against an AlphaZero‑like agent where the skill level is adjusted using a temperature parameter; it is not clear if adaptive search provides a unique advantage over simply adjusting the exploration‑exploitation balance in standard MCTS.
